title: The death of the brave
hookLine: death is the right of the brave, if it is accepted in the Lord's court (Vadhans M1, ang 579)

cards: People who work in hospice sometimes say the same thing: there's a difference between someone who dies afraid and someone who dies ready. Not braver in the movie sense. Just settled.
They've said what they needed to say. They've made their peace. Most of us don't like to think about it at all.
We change the subject, knock on wood, scroll past. Guru Nanak's second lament doesn't change the subject. It says there's such a thing as a good death, and it says who gets one.

teach.b: The second of Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa, on Ang five seventy-nine, has a line Sikhs know well. In paraphrase: death is the right of the brave, of true heroes, if their death is accepted.
And nearby: don't call death bad, people, if one knows how to truly die.
The word for the brave is sooraa, a hero, a warrior.

But look who the hymn says the heroes are: they alone are called brave who receive honor in the true court. They leave with honor, and are honored when they arrive. So bravery here isn't measured by the battlefield.
It's measured by acceptance in the dargah, the Lord's court. What makes a death accepted? The hymn's answer, and the Granth's answer everywhere, is a life lived remembering the Name, serving, honest.
The death of the brave is the end of a brave life, one that didn't flinch from truth. That's why these lines mean so much to a community with many martyrs.
Sikhs remember Guru Arjan, Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Tenth Guru's sons, and countless others who faced death without giving up their faith.
But the hymn belongs just as much to a grandmother dying in her bed, having lived kindly and remembered God. Her death, too, is the death of the brave.
One more word: parvaan, accepted, approved, signed off. It's the key to the line. The question isn't how you die.
It's whether the life it ends is accepted.

how: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa at funerals and remembrances, and these lines on the death of the brave are often recalled when martyrs are remembered.

o: a soldier who wins every battle
someone with no fear of anything
a hero, brave in how life is lived

games.q: the death of the brave — tap the pairs.
p: a hero, one who is brave

s: the hymn says only warriors die the death of the brave
bravery is measured by acceptance in the Lord's court, after a true life.
the lament says don't call death bad, if one knows how truly to die
a good death is the end of a life lived remembering the Name.

games.q: you want to know who the hymn calls truly brave. what's the test?
o: whether they receive honor in the true court.
games.why: they alone are called brave who are honored in the Lord's court: they leave with honor and arrive with honor.

practice: Think of the next hour of your day, and what it would look like lived bravely in this hymn's sense: not dramatic, just true, the honest answer, the patient word, the thing you've been avoiding.
Choose one, and picture yourself doing it calmly. If you pray, say Waheguru, and ask to live this hour in a way that would be accepted.

wordCard.voice: Sooraa, a hero, a warrior: Guru Nanak's lament says death is the right of the sooraa, if it's accepted in the Lord's court; don't call death bad, if one knows how truly to die.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a hero, a brave one; in the lament, the brave are those accepted in the court.

carryVoice: Your line: accepted in his court. Bravery is measured by how a life is lived. Six hundred seventy-five days in.
